1.	Why have Griffenhagen and Associates been appointed to investigate the Post Office Department?
2.	Is it true that the Government have agreed to pay that firm $10,000 a month for said investigation?
3.	How many German Americans are members of the above firm?
4.	Could not a British or a Canadian firm have been employed for such an investigation?

1.	This firm has been retained by the Government to assist in reorganization work because of its wide experience in the investigation and reorganization of governmental departments, public bodies and industrial establishments in the United States and Canada. It has a trained staff composed in part of Canadians which specializes in efficiency and reorganization work, including the study and survey of departmental organization, accounting and offi.ce procedure, methods of work, and the installation of organization, records, and procedure that a long experience in this work has shown to be best adapted to economical and efficient administration of Government departments as required in the public interest.
2.	The firm is to be paid at the rate of $10,.000 per month for a stated number of experts, working in conjunction with the Deputy Head and other selected officials of the department concerned. The investigation, however, includes other depatments than the Post Office.
3.	None.
4.	There is no firm in Canada with wide experience in this kind of work. This firm is familiar with conditions in the 'Canadian Service because of its work during a year or more under the Civil Service Commission, and has thus acquired a knowledge of the problems arising in the administration of various departments. The work of reclassification has brought it into more or less close contact with the departments, and disclosed many of the weaknesses that it is

proposed to remedy. No other concern, known to the Government, is so well fitted by its long experience in the investigation and reorganization of industrial and public bodies, as well as its immediate contact with problems encountered in the administration of the Government of Canada. Any other firm would be under the disadvantage of having to spend a long period of nonproductive time to become familiar with the conditions throughout the service. The reorganization of the Department of Public Printing and Stationery has shown the possibilities of improvement in the service that may be expected through them.

speechtext: The House resumed from May 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. 12 (Hon. Mr. Guthrie) respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When progress was reported upon this Bill on Monday, May 17, paragraph (k) of clause 2, clauses 32, 63 and 101 with the amendment proposed by the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) had been allowed to stand. All of the other

clauses had been agreed to with the exception of clauses 19 and 76 which cannot be considered until the House has concurred in the required money resolution. Clause 32 had been discussed at length and was still before the committee. Shall clause 32 carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think we might first make an amendment which has been agreed upon to clause 100 in regard to advance polls.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Guthrie moves by unanimous consent that clause 100 be now reconsidered. Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the motion?
Mofion .agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The amendment I desire to move, Mr. Chairman, is as follows:
In clause 100, in line one, insert "and" between "sailor" and "commercial" and in line two strike out "or other person."
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think we have dealt with section 101. If not I would move to reconsider it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Clause 101 is still open.
That is about the Canada Temperance Act is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that clause 101 as printed in the Bill be struck out and the following be substituted therefore:
101. Whenever under the Canada Temperance Act a vote is to be taken, the procedure to be followed shall, in lieu of the procedure therein directed, be the procedure laid down in this Act with such modifications as the Chief Electoral Officer may direct as being necessary by reason of the difference in the nature of the question to be submitted, and with such omissions as he may specify on the ground that compliance with the procedure laid down is not required.
(2)	Any direction given by the Chief Electoral Officer for a modification of or omission from the procedure directed by this Act shall be published by him in the Canada Gazette at least four weeks before the day upon which the vote is to be taken.
(3)	Notwithstanding anything in this Act, the list of voters as finally revised and completed for use in the Provincial eleotion in the province of Ontario, held in the month of October, 1919, shall be used without revision for any vote in that province under this section taken before the 31st day of December, 1920.
I may say, Mr. Chairman, that Ithe difficulty under the section as first drawn is this:	In the Canada Temperance Amendment Act passed in 1919 certain provisions were incorporated in the amendment in regard to the taking of the vote. One that

occurs to me at the present dime is that the hours of the polling are stated in the amendment, and those hours are the old hours between nine o'clock in Ithe morning and five o'clock in the afternoon. Representations have been made that these hours are not, under modern conditions, sufficient to enable all 'the votes of men and women to be polled either at an election or a referendum, and the persons making the representations prefer that the new hours proposed in the presenlt Bill be adopted for the purpose of the referendum.
Then there is a great deal of unnecessary machinery in the present Bill if you try to apply it merely to a referendum vote. All Ithe provisions about nominations of candidates, and so on, that will not be applicable to simply the referendum vote. So that in order to adapt Ithe machinery in the present Bill to a referendum vote it is necessary that it should undergo some modification and the proposal is simply this: That when a vote is to be taken on a referendum, the machinery of the present Bill shall be the machinery under which the vote is taken. If in any case ilt is not adapted to the referendum, the Chief Electoral Office has power so to decide, and his decision is to be published four weeks before the vote in the Canada Gazette.
The other question that is covered in this amendment is the vote to be taken in the province of Ontario next autumn. As the House is aware there was a provincial list prepared in that province last October. I do' not think that it will be officially one year old by the date contemplated for the referendum volte; it may be a day or two more or a day or two less than that, but it will be in the neighbourhood of twelve months since the list was finally completed. It has been considered that in order to avoid expense that list might be deemed absolute and complete for -the purpose of the referendum vote. Any representations that have been made to me have been in favour of such a course. It was a provincial list of recent adaptation, or preparation, and I have heard no objection-no serious objection at all events-to the course proposed, and thalt course would certainly save all the cost of preparing new lists for that important or unimportant event. I therefore move, Mr. Chairman, that the clause be amended in the way indicated in the amendment I have just read.

Before you put the
amendment may I put a question. The clause as it stood in the Bill we are now 245i
passing, would apply in full in case of a referendum under the Canada Temperance Act. Under the amendment I understand that it will be left to the Chief Electoral Officer to determine what parts of the Act are to apply and what parts are to be omitted. Do I understand rightly?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He will determine what parts of the Act have to be modified.
He is to have the right to make modifications?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The amendment proposes that the Act shall apply, but that if in certain cases it has to be modified, the Chief Electoral Officer shall make the necessary modifications and publish them in the Canada Galzette four weeks before the voting date. It is only in minor cases that trouble could arise. In our Act we fix a certain time within which certain things are to be done, such as the nomination of candidates, the revision of lists, and so on-things which will not apply in an ordinary referendum vote. This amendment is proposed in order to clarify the matter and give the Chief Electoral Officer power to say what modifications are necessary.
Is the restriction about the Ontario lists made because of the understanding that in certain cities if the lists were two years old they could not be used?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, this is independent of that understanding. This is merely for the purpose of avoiding throughout the province of Ontario the preparation of. new lists for the purpose of this Bill. There is one clerical error in the amendment as you read it, Mr. Chairman. In subsection 3 the phrase "general election in the province," should be "provincial election in the province."
Call it "general provincial election."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think we should call it "provincial." We always , carry in our minds the distinction between a provincial and a general election.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This is entirely apart
from the matter raised by my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), which will come under section 32. I see no objection to providing in that section that lists up to two years old may be used as the basis. That was suggested by my hon. friend in regard to certain cities in the province of Quebec-
Five cities.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Where there was a revision of the lists every two years. I think the two-year qualification might apply throughout Canada-tout we have not come to that section yet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When this section was held over for further consideration I think it was felt that if the machinery to be used was the machinery set forth in the Act as now drafted, it would be very expensive for taking the vote under the Canada Temperance Act. On the other hand, if the Bill as it .stands is to be amended on the lines previously discussed here so as to make the lists already prepared for the provinces apply for federal purposes. I think there would be no objection to passing this section now. But I am assuming that the minister intends to consider the amendments which he placed on Hansard, and will take them up in committee; and I am assuming also that they will meet with the approval of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think when the House last discussed the question I stated very distinctly that these were merely suggestions, that they were not moved as amendments, and my hon. friend must not go on the assumption that I in any way intend to abide by them. They do not affect the question under discussion. No matter what we decide under section 32, we must assume that a vote will have to be taken in two, and perhaps three provinces this fall; nnd this is only a general clause to avoid as far as possible any difficulty between administration under this Act and the Canada Temperance Act. For instance, the ballot papers will be different; there will be no names of candidates, but the electors will be asked to vote for or against the memorandum; the instructions to voters will be different; the sample Bill will be different; the forms of oath have to be changed; these are matters which we think we can safely leave to the Chief Electoral Officer, particularly when he has to give four weeks' notice in the Canada Gazette of any changes he makes.
I think the power is too broad. The Chief Electoral Officer might make any modifications he likes and who-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Any necessary modification.

There is no control even by the Governor in Council or by the Secre-

tary of State and the Chief Electoral Officer becomes the absolute court of last resort. True he publishes any modifications or omissions in the Official Gazette. But supposing he does where is the remedy. Any complainant can only go to the Chief Electoral Officer and if the Chief Electoral Officer chooses to consider the complaint he mav but otherwise the complainant's remedy is exhausted. If there was some authority over the Chief Electoral Officer, then the party feeling aggrieved would have the satisfaction of appealing to that higher authority. Tit seems to me that vesting this absolute power in the Chief Electoral Officer is not good policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He has not absolute power.
There is no one to restrict him.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He has power only to make such modifications ais may be necessary to adapt this Act to the special conditions. I can see another way of accomplishing the same purpose, but I think it will take three or four weeks to do it; we will just have to pass duplicate sections and make special provisions for everything we do under the Election Act.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is only in some minor respects that there can be any conflict.
We can fix it by making the action of the Chief Electoral Officer subject to the approval of the Governor in Council or the Secretary of State.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think it would be better to make the Chief Electoral Officer supreme than to make him subordinate to the Secretary of State or the Government. The idea was to leave the matter in charge of a man
s far as possible removed from political influence.
Some contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Now Mr. Chairman, if I might discuss clause 76, leaving clause 32 in the meantime? I will inform the House of the reason.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Clause 76 can be discussed, but it cannot be adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the point. It is in order to determine some principle upon

which this question may he settled so that I may introduce the necessary resolution for consideration of the committee, as this clause will involve the expenditure of public money.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Very good. Clause 76 

Fees and expenses of election officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The difficulty, I may
point out, is this. We have sought to establish >a scale of fees for all officers who take part in the work of an election, and the difficulty has arisen from the fact that all constituencies are not alike. Difficulties have to be overcome in some of the remote constituencies which are not met with in ordinary city constituencies; consequently the fees payable in outlying districts should be more than those payable in compact, settled constituencies in the older provinces. One scale of fees will not give general satisfaction. Information is forthcoming, particularly in regard to the referendum votes which are contemplated during the coming fall, that returning officers and deputy returning officers cannot be secured at anything like the old scale of fees. It has been pointed out to me that in some ridings in New Brunswick and tihie Yukon and in some of the more remote parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta a considerable increase of fees is necesary in order to procure the necessary officials, and the same thing will have to be done in the unorganized districts of Ontario and in some constituencies in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. So the proposal is that instead of settling upon one scale of fees for the whole of Canada the Chief Electoral Officer siball himself fix a scale of fees after making full inquiry into the circumstances pertaining to each electoral district. He will have to have in his office a pretty full record of each riding. He will have to know all the cities, towns and villages in each riding, the population and the distances, and he will be the person best able, I think, to prescribe a satisfactory schedule of fees. So that the proposal I make to the committee is that the clause as printed in the Bill be not adopted but that a new clause to this effect be adopted:
Upon the recommendation of the Chief Electoral Officer, the Governor General in Counci' may take a tariff of fees, costs, allowances, and expenses to be paid and allowed to returning officers and other persons employed at or with respect to elections under this Act, and may from time to time revise and amend such tariff.
That would be to omit subsections 1, 2 and 3 as now drawn and to allow 4, 5, 6, and 7 to stand with the addition of the clause
that I have just read. If that arrangement-meets with the approval of the committee I can have a resolution introduced along these lines. We cannot pass section 7!>
until a resolution has been adopted in the committee, and I think it would be well to settle upon some policy in Tegard to the matter. I have no special policy to offer; I merely suggest this as the most practical way of settling a difficult question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It depends
very much upon who is appointed as Chief Electoral Officer and how he is to be chosen. Has the minister any information to give the committee on that point5

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I might be able to give it if the Chief Whip for the other side were Were. There was to be a conference this morning and there will be one this afternoon as soon as my hon. friend's representative returns. In the meantime, I do not know that the matter is definitely settled. However, I assure the committee that the man selected as Chief Electoral Officer will be some outstanding person in whom the House has confidence. A number of names have been discussed, but no final determination has yet been reached.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the minister intend to regard this appointment as one to be made by the Government of its own volition, or does he intend to have any conference on the subject one way or the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is an appointment which the Government must settle ultimately and for which it must take the responsibility, although; I think it is advisable that the Government should consult before finally settling upon any definite appointment. But as in all cases the ultimate responsibility for the selection must rest with the Government. If the principle I now advocate be adopted, I can proceed to give notice so that there may be no delay in getting the matter into the committee stage. I can well understand that when we come to section 19, which has regard to the appointment of <a Chief Electoral Officer, this proposal concerning fees will be urged as one of the reasons why we must have an absolutely fair and impartial and outstanding man for that position.

Will the scale of fees
be recommended to the Governor in Council for each general election?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that ilt
would be a permanent scale of fees, because there is no doubt that at the present time we have to pay more than alfc any other time in the country's history. That condition may not continue. The clause as drawn would give the Chief Electoral Offi-[DOT]>eer power to make recommendations from time to time. I think he would have to make five or six different scales of fees, one to apply in cities; one in semi-urban and semi-rural ridings, compact in size and distance; another in ridings totally rural; another in unsettled portions of Canada where the distances are very great. All these matters will have Ito be considered and some scale adopted which will apply to groups of constituencies which are similarly situated.

I quite approve of the
suggestion made by the minister. For instance, the county of Gloucester, which I have the honour to represent, has a coast two hundred miles in length, and includes two islands, Miscou island and Shippigan island. Alt certain times of the year, especially in spring and fall, it becomes very difficult to cross the harbours and to gain access to these islands. Particularly is this the case when, as very often happens, the election is held lalte in the year. During the last five or six elections there have been complaints from the returning officers that the fees allowed were not sufficient. The suggestion made by the minister, therefore, will be heartily approved by the people of the north shore of New Brunswick.
Mr.	MOW AT:	I am quite sure
that the returning officer in the country has a great	deal to do. But

With respect to an elector voting at an advance poll the suggestion was made, and taken under consideration, as to whether he should not be obliged to take an oath instead of simply signing the form TT found at page 110.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not think it was
necessary. The elector gets his certificate from the proper officer who has a right to issue those certificates and who can swear him. Then when he comes to vote the possession of the certificate will be sufficient.
Some other man may take the certificate and use it. The elector has got to sign anyway so where is the harm of adopting some precaution?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You can swear the man as he comes up in the ordinary way as yon can any voter.
Then what is the use of putting this in at all. The elector has to sign his name on the certificate of identification so why not have him sworn. What is the objection?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am told the object of that is to make sure that you have the right man. When he gets a certificate he has to sign his signature just as the banks require when they issue foreign bank cheques. When the elector goes to vote the officials can say, "Let us see your signature," and they can compare it Tight here.
I cannot see any reason for not making the change suggested if you want a real safeguard.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think this is the procedure followed by the express companies when they issue money orders, as well as by the banks in the case of foreign cheques.
But this is very important.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it can be better safeguarded than by the signature proposals.

In connection with Form UU, it is stated explicitly that the declaration provided for there is not made under oath. Very well, why not have the elector make the declaration under oath. If a man cannot vote except at an advance poll why not

require him to take an oath that his calling is such that he cannot vote at any other time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not see why you should swear a railway man more than any other individual; I think that a railway man's vote should be taken as readily as anybody else's. This applies only to three classes of people and I would not impose upon them the necessity of taking an oath to get the ordinary rights to which they are entitled. We are safeguarding it in every possible way.

This is a special privilege accorded to certain classes of men be-clause they will be absent from their homes on polling day. Does my hon. friend claim that if a man's name is not on the list he should not have to swear in order to be allowed to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He certainly will.

He may be as honest a man as any hon. member or any railway conductor. Why do you do it? Because that man is getting -a special privilege. Here is a man who is going to vote in advance of the election. To that extent he is getting a special privilege, and I contend that the argument put forward by my hon. friend is absolutely right, that he ought to swear that he is coming within the provisions of the Act giving him that privilege; otherwise his vote ought not to be taken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is not a
question of doubting the word of the railway men, it is really protecting them against impostors.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: How does this work out? In the first place a man has to be on the voters' list. He goes to the presiding officer and says, "I want a certificate to enable me to vote at the advance polls," and as part of the procedure to avoid any "double crossing" we make him sign his name at the bottom of that certificate in the presence of .the returning officer. He goes to the advance poll, and he is bound by every oath prescribed under the law and can be sworn. What more swearing is necessary? We have double identification, we have the oath, we have the fact that his name is on the list, and we have his signature. Why don't you swear all the agents that go out to vote? They get special privileges.
I may go to the returning officer and sign "Hugh Guthrie" instead of "Jacques Bureau." That is no evidence that I am the Minister of Militia.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: People do not do that sort of thing. We are prescribing the safeguard that every bank in the country uses.
If this is necessary at all-

On section 32, I think it would he the wisest for us to pursue the policy as originally drawn and submitted Ito the House. It has been very carefully examined by the officers of the Government and by some gentlemen who are expert in such matters. There are clerical errors in it as printed. It is true there have been a great many suggestions of various kinds. We had a conference of members representing both sides of the House wilth a view to seeing if we could not arrive at some satisfactory basis upon which we could all agree. Apparently that is not possible. The difficulties ahead of us are such thalt we cannot reconcile them all. I think it would he far better to adopt one general principle for the whole of Canada than to make exceptions here and (there for this province or that province. The scheme which was originally adopted when the Bill was framed was to adopt a general principle throughout Canada. As the committee is aware, the principle upon which the Bill was framed was that all the provincial lists should be adopted on the basis of the franchise in any province where there was a provincial list not more than twelve months old. I think that was a good principle. But it has been poinlted out that in one particular province there are five or six cities where there is not an annual list but

where there is a list prepared every two years and that is in Ithe province of Quebec. It seems Ithat in that province there is an annual lis-t save in the case of five or six cities w'here there is only a biennial list. The hon. member for IThree Rivers (Mr. Bureau) desires that difficulty to be obviated and I see no reason against doing it by making a general provision to the effect that we will accept as the basis .of our franchise the lists of all Ithe provinces were not more than two years old. If in any province there is no list which is not more than two years of age a new list will have to be prepared from beginning to end but if we have a lislt in any province not more than two years of age we will take that list as the basis, carrying it forward under the provisions of section 32 as laid down in this Aot. It will give us uniformity in every province of Canada. The only question, upon which I think there might be some criticism is perhaps on the question of expense. It is going to be a fairly expensive Act to administer but I believe it will give us as complete, as up to date and as honest and fair .a voters' list as we have ever had in this country. For these reasons, if we have a little extra expense, we can well afford it. It is only every four or five years that Ithe machinery under this Act is put in operation. Spread the expense over four or five years and it does not appear to be so great. Suggestions which were made when we had our conference in May were that in the rural divisions-not urban, because we propose no change there-but in rural divisions where there were lists in existence which were not more than two years of age there should be no registrar or enumerator appointed to prepare lists; in other words that we should adopt the provincial lists giving persons whose names had been omitted Ithe right to appeal to the county judge or revising officer to have their names included but giving them the power which we undoubtedly give them under section 63 to go to the returning officer on election day, .obtain a ballot and volte. That would relieve us of the necessity of appointing a large number of rural registrars. But if it should happen that an election came on when there were no lists under two years of age we would have to undergo the expense anyway. In twelve divisions and in the unorganized territories of Ontario; in some in Quebec; and in some in British Columbia we would have to undergo the expense anyway. Because in those cases they have no lists-no up-to-date 246
lists-there is a floating population in those places and there must be an enumeration if-
There is no part of the province of Quebec in that condition now.

One can only believe that the Government must be actuated by one of two reasons in the stand which it takes in regard to this matter. The other is that- they wish in some way to confuse the electors so that men who have been put on these provincial lists will think their names are still on, but will find on election day that the provincial list is not used at all and that it is only the list
prepared by the registrar that is to be used as the basis for voting. Anything that is going to create a lack of confidence or a lack of certainty in the mind of the electorate is going to lead to the feeling that Parliament is not truly representative of the will of the people. Anything that the Government can do to establish confidence and to effect economy in the preparation of the voters' lists is most- necessary at this time.

I am of the opinion that in so far as it is possible the lists of each province should be adopted as final. They are recognized as fair and just. I am led to this conclusion because of the circumstances in the constituency which I represent. In my opinion the list of each province should be adopted as final for federal purposes and we should get rid of enumerators or registrars. My reason for this proposition is that I recognize the lists of each province as fair and just and that they have been carefully prepared by the proper authority in each province. By adopting these provincial lists we will save great expense and in the end we will have a fair list. TheActing Solicitor General tells us that the Government want to adopt provincial lists as a basis for the federal lists in each constituency. I do not understand what he means by our adopting those lists as a basis; does he want us to believe that these lists will be taken as original lists? Take for example a list that has been prepared in the province of Quebec and on which the names of men only appear as voters. Then I say that if there are 200 names on this list the enumerator or the registrar will be called upon to place on that list at least 100 or 150 names of women. I do not think that in such circumstances that you could possibly take the list prepared in the province of Quebec as a basis for the federal voters' lists. I have been opposed to woman suffrage; I am still opposed to it and I think the public sentiment of the province of Quebec is against it. In the preparation of these federal lists I think we should look to what has already been decided upon by each province in respect to this list and adopt the provincial lists as final.

Would the minister not consider the fact that in the final analysis if this list having your own board or appointees to hear the appeals you would be amply protected? As I understand it, the lists in Nova Scotia are called provincial lists, while the lists in Ontario are called muni-

cipal lists. They are the same thing. It you were to take the provincial lists as they are now, no matter hy what name you call them, and you appoint your own board to revise those lists how can the Government possibly be prejudiced? Would the minister not be saved a lot of trouble by simply accepting those lists? Let them be treated as the lists for federal purposes and let us go on using them. It appears to me that would be the proper thing to do. The minister says we are not very far apart and yet we are. When we come to analyse the matter, it simply means that the whole difference is as between a provincial list and a municipal list; but if upon that municipal list elections are to be held the only difference between us now is the fact that such lists are municipal lists until an election is held upon them. Then they are regarded as provincial lists. Well, in what respect does that matter, because the whole of the necessary process has been gone through to put them in the shape of provincial lists and they are only municipal lists in name only. The sole difference between us appears to be that an election must be held upon them.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There is more than
that.

Let me suggest to the minister that if he appoints his own board, if he revises those lists-after having been already revised under the Ontario Act- surely he has riveted, and doubly riveted- every advantage he could possibly have, and furthermore he is saving a lot of trouble and expense. He will have the power to add to or subtract from that list; and furthermore, as pointed out by the leader of the Opposition, where an elector has been left off the list one man can now vouch for him and enable him to vote. I cannot see the force of the ministers argument. I cannot see what objection there can be to saying that these lists shall be provincial lists after they have been completed by the municipalities and that they shall then be regarded as Ontario lists.
Even the Ontario Government itself does not at present accept those lists as provincial lists.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend and I do not view this question from the same angle.
Perhaps not.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition suggested a few minutes ago that

we should allow one man instead of two to do the vouching for a voter and that has been passed. As I understand, the section was put in to safeguard the rights and interests of hon. members opposite, not the interests of hon. gentlemen on this side. The suggestion was that on this side we had the machinery and we had the officials and the provision in question was adopted to guard against any wrong doing on their part. The safeguard was certainly not to protect any interests of hon. gentlemen on this side; it was adopted to protect the interests of hon. gentlemen opposite
Now the point at issue between us at the present time is this:	Before the Ontario Vdters' List Act was brought in at the recent session of the legislature, our Bill was introduced into this House, and certain sections from our Bill were copied into the provincial enactment. We started on the principle that we would adopt the provincial lists and we abide by it. If the Ontario Government have not a provincial list how can we remedy Ithat? And they have not. My hon. friend even says they have not; I am able to take it for granted that they have not. My hon. friend says that in all the either provinces it is all right to adopt the provincial lists, but there is not one in Ontario so therefore in that province we should take the municipal lists. I would ndt be opposed to taking a municipal list if there was such a thing, but there is not, and there will be no municipal lists until a year from next autumn. Those lists will not possibly even be revised until a year from nexlt December.

The returns are usually in
by the 15th of April.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
They may get some of
them but in some instances the revision does not take place until June, and in others not unltil July or August, and when there is delay the work is thrown over until September or October.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why does the minister object if the preparation of the lists are going Ito occupy that long?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In all human probability there would not be a provincial list available for general elections purposes this year if required. I do not want to make exceptions. I do not see why we should declare for the principle of -adopting provincial voters lists for federal purposes and then make an exception because one province, knowing that, says "We -shall not have provincial voters' lists and there-

fore we must prepare our own lislts." Still,
I would have no objection to adopting the list prepared under the Ontario legislation of last session with this provision:	That
in all olther respects we add to or take from them by virtue of the provisions of section 32. Now under section 32 there is no power of revision in rural communities, that power is given only in urban districts. The only power that can add Ito or take from the lists in a rural community is the rural registrar. With the provisions of section 32 remaining intadt in. that respect I would not object Ito taking such voters' lists as are prepared under the Act recently passed by the Ontario Legislature, provided that at any time there are such lists that could be made available here. But honestly I do not know how you are going to define such lislts. When do the first lists that could be available come into force? I am satisfied they do not come into force until [DOT]a year from next autumn which would be 1921. Then if an election were held between 1921 and 1923 those lislts might be used as a basis for federal lists, and if the same power were given, as is given under section 32, to add to or take from them, I would not be opposed to accepting fthat list, but I would not call them municipal lists. It was suggested to me that such a lislt might be called a list which was to be the basis of a provincial list.
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not have any
objection Ito that. But let us be clear on this point. I think I rather misunderstood what my hon. friend said in the first instance. If he now thinks thalt is going to avoid the appointment of rural registrars he is very much mistaken, because the rural registrars are Ithe men who are to add to and take from the lists.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As I said a
moment ago the question of phraseology is quite secondary.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I would like you to
suggest your phraseology because for the life of me I do not see how you are going to frame ilt.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would be
very glad to make a suggestion. I think if the minister will add just a paragraph to section 32-or he could put it in the interpretation clause if he likes-that "provincial lists" for the province of Ontario shall mean the lists that have been prepared by the assessors and revised by the courts of revision;-that will cover all that I have
in mind on this point. I think that goes as far as my hon. friend considers now that he has a right to go.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Any language such as my hon. friend has just suggested would hot be of any use at all. We would then find ourselves in the predicament that there would be no lists of that kind available, and then we would have to start at the preparation of the lists de novo.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the lists are available why is my hon. friend objecting?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If we are going to accomplish our purpose we must frame a language that will mean something. There must be some particular list in view or we will land nowhere. How would my hon. friend deal with language such as this, which is clear and distinct:
For the purposes of any ^Dominion election held within the limits of a province the voters' lists shall be those prepared and completed for the several polling divisions under the laws of that province within two years immediately preceding the issue of the Writ for such election and which were, under such taws in force, or had been last in force, for the purpose of provincial elections.
Now what change would my hon. friend make?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should add words to the effect that they shall be deemed to be in force if they have been prepared by the assessors and revised by the courts of revision as set forth in the provincial law. The only point of difference between us, as has often been said from this side, is this: If my hon. friend says that these lists "are in force" only when they have once been used for a provincial election it is perfectly obvious it will be four years before any advantage can be taken of the lists as prepared under the Ontario Act. On the other hand if he does not place that interpretation upon the provision but will take as a basis for the federal lists the lists that have been made up by the assessors and revised by these courts of revision, that meets our point.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Those lists would not be a basis. Because my hon. friend will see that they are not the provincial voters' lists. . Under the Ontario Act the lists he refers to are not 'provincial voters' lists. They have to be further revised. It ds notorious, it is well understood, that the municipal lists do not include parliamentary voters. It is supposed that the assessor will cover all the voters that he can but he does not exert

himself to do so; the predominant idea with him is to gather a list of 'municipal voters. Those lists do not become provincial lists until they are finally revised for that purpose. What my hon. friend asks me to do is to accept lists which the Ontario Government may regard as a basis for the provincial lists, but they are not in the true sense of the term such lists as would form a basis for a federal voters' list.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are we going to have municipal lists in the other provinces? I think no exception would be taken in the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot agree to that. The only reason I considered it in this case is because the Ontario Legislature has in its wisdom not seen fit for some purposes to have provincial voters' lists. But if this means throughout Canada that you are going to adopt some other principle, and change the principle of the Bill which we have discussed here for some three or four months, I cannot agree.

Would it not be possible for my hon. friend to adopt some such provision in regard to amending these incomplete lists, as was suggested in page 3 of the memorandum. There does not seem to be very much difference between us here. If my hon. friend insists upon the appointment of enumerators all over the province of Ontario, it does not seem to me that we shall be saving expense. If he is willing to take what he says in the assessment roll prepared by the assessor and revised by the municipal court of revision and then by the judge, as under the old Ontario law, and to change the phraseology and take that as the basis of the provincial lists, he will then have complete lists, and he can have them revised as the Ontario Act provides by the board of revision, or if that is unsatisfactory to him he can have them revised in accordance with his own suggestions as extended on Hansard of May 17. If the reviser in a neighbouring urban-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That was before you threw in the monkey wrench.

I did not throw in the monkey wrench. My hon. friend said he was willing to receive suggestions, and the suggestion I have just put forward was made by the gentleman whom my hon. friend left in charge of the conference which I attended. Any monkey wrench came from the other side of the House. But that is not the point. If my hon. friend is willing to take what he has just suggested as the basis

of the lists, what is it going to mean? It means having enumerators appointed in every electoral district to the number of fifty or a hundred, to add probably in one polling subdivision two or three names, and in other subdivisions none at all, and he will have to pay them from $50 to $100 apiece. Why cannot he adopt his own suggestion and say that those lists shall be taken and named as he said they might be named and revised by a revioing officer appointed by him in the urban municipalities? He will save a lot of trouble, and the impression will go abroad throughout the country that he is trying to prepare fair and honest lists, and he will accomplish everything he is attempting to do under the Act.

I do not think the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Ross) is attempting to mislead the House, but he knows as well as any hon. member from Ontario that at the present time less than one-half of the electors are on the provincial lists. No women are included except property owners and tax-payers. The Ontario Government repealed part 3 of the municipal owners' lists which did contain a considerable percentage of Dominion voters. At the present time the only ones whose names appear on those lists are the tax-payers of the municipality. The same thing will apply next year in spite of the fact that the Ontario Government has passed a Voters' List Bill. The Act does not apply until December of next year, and in the meantime we will have voters' lists exactly similar to those which we have at the present time. It would be absolutely foolish to attempt to add to those lists fully 50 per cent of the names that should be on them for federal election purposes by having those people go to some urban municipality many miles away. In Northern Ontario it would be absolutely impossible to carry on in that way. The lists prepared years ago in the province of Ontario were very good lists and very little work would be required to complete them, but to amend the present lists is out of the question.	i |

The Court of Revision deals with the assessment roll, and the roll is completed and returned to the council, then it is printed and published and appeals can be made to the county judge. No appeals may ever be put in. But no one will pretend to say that the names of all the electors are on that list. Then who is going to put them on? The whole point seems to me to hinge upon this: Who will do that

work? My hon. friends on the other side say it can he done a great deal cheaper as they suggest; I doubt it very much. The leader of the Opposition must surely be mistaken when he states that the election of 1917 was a fraudulent one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Oh, no.
I think I know just as much as he does about thait election, and I throw back tihe insinuation. I say if there ever was a fair vote ilt was in the election of 1917.
The people were not given a chance to poll their votes. It was a robbery. Call it by its name

As I understand, the minister says he would be willing under certain circumstances to 'accept 'the municipal lists as the basis. If he did accept those lists- and the municipal lists I 'am speaking of noiw are complete in Bill details, having gone before the Court of Revision judge-the Government would "then only need to appoint one registrar in, each riding to be the final Court of Revision to 'add to or subtract from those lists as made up.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want it to be understood that I ever said I would accept municipal lists.
I was not putting woTds in your mouth. 1 said I "understood."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I aim opposed to municipal lists. But there is this to he said: under the Act which was passed at the last session of the Ontario Legislature, intituled "An Act respecting Elections and the preparation of Provincial Voters' Lists," and the short title of which is, "Thj Election Laws Amendment Act," the lists to be prepaired 'apply to provincial elections. But I do not think we should be asked to accept half-baked lists. There are the lists made by the 'assessors the preparation of which will be started next spring, and they will be revised by (the Court of Revision in the municipality 'and by the county judge; those are your municipal lists. But those are not provincial lists under this Act.
When do they become provincial lists?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: After they have been further revised 'by the Board of Revisers under this Ontario Act, that is prior to a provincial election; and the revisers have not yet been appointed. Now, my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) insisted on the same thing during the previous debate. He said, "I want you to accept these municipal lists in Ontario." That makes an exception as -against all the other provinces and changes the principle of our Act. Why should we do it in Ontario? We have at this moment the provincial voters' lists which were vooed on last October, they will be good under this law fbtr two years. We will have to accept them as the basis for the next two years-

Will my hon. friend permit me a question? At the end of two- years when the present election law is superseded, and there is no election in the province of Ontario, have we any lists for that province? I am asking for information.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether we will or not. It depends how they work under this Act, whether they want a provincial election or not. I do not know what the Drury Government intend to do. But if there are no lists, we have to prepare them under section 32; and if there are lists, we have 'to 'adopt them under that section. But in the meantime I cannot see any good ground for saying, "Yon shall take what is not yet prepared, hiit which we hope next year will be prepared, and which will be only municipal lists." Where I met my hon. friend [DOT], and where I though perhaps we were together at one time was this: (that if we accept those lists in future in Ontario-'lists that do not exist now, and which at the end of next year will ibe municipal lists pure and simple- , if we accept those 'as the basis, we know they will not be complete for federal purposes, and they should 'be subject to the revision provided by section 32, which involves the appointment of rural registrars to do thait work. In cities, towns 'and villages we follow the Act exactly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do I understand, then, that if we on this side are agreeable to the minister's appointing his own registrars to revise the lists, whatever lists they may be, he will agree to accept as lists, so far as Ontario is concerned, the municipal lists prepared under the Ontario laws.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I will not call them
municipal lists.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Let me put it in another way. The Ontario law is a law providing lists for electoral purposes. In the operation of that law there are three stages in the preparation of lists so far as the procedure is concerned. There is first the preparation by assessors, then the revision by a court of revision, and finally re-

vision before an election. The Drury Government came into office in 1919; it will continue in office for four years, say until 1923. If my hon. friend regards as provincial lists in Ontario only lists that are made available for an election in Ontario, then the Ontario lists will be of no service so far as a Dominion election is concerned; it will be 1923 before the Ontario lists will have any significance one way or the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That would be about
right, would it not?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It might from the point of view of some hon. gentlemen opposite; I do not think it would from the point of view of the country and its interests. On the other hand, if my hon. friend is prepared to take the lists as prepared by the assessors under this -Provincial Act and revised by courts of revision, that being an annual process, and to regard that annual list as the basis for the purposes of a federal election, being the basis of the provincial lists under the Ontario Act, as I understand' it-if my hon. friend will do that we will meet him on the point of allowing him to choose his own revising officers. That will bring us both together, we on our side conceding that the Government shall appoint its own revising officers and the Government meeting us to the extent of using as a basis for revision the lists as prepared under this Act and revised according to the stages I have mentioned. There is this limitation, however: I think my hon. friend will feel it to be in the public interest that some limit be placed on the number of registrars who shall be required for the purpose of revising these lists. . My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Pardee) has suggested that there be one registrar for the revision of lists in each electoral district. That would limit the number and would certainly help to create public confidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend has considered the working out of this proposed machinery. One man would not have a chance at all. We tried it in British Columbia last fall. As a rule, when people are required to do a thing within a certain number of days they wait until the last day and the result is that the courts are overcrowded, the people cannot get their applications in and consequently do not get their names on the list. I do not believe that you could get along with less than one man for each rural polling subdivision, assuming, as I assume that there will be from three to four hundred names to the division, including the names of women, of course.

All -these officials will have to be there; whether you work them the whole of the four or the five days is anoter matter. You might cut down the number of days that they shall sit, reducing the expense by half. The Act provides five days; that may be too long; they might do it in two days or in three days at most. But I do not think that you can have less than one to each polling subdivision if you are to have regard at all to the rights and convenience of the people. I am willing to try to frame a clause on the lines suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) expressly on the condition that the list that we recognize as a basic list is a provincial list, though only in course of preparation, not finally completed for provincial purposes. But I will not recognize a proposal that involves our accepting municipal lists as a basis, because if that principle is applied to one part of Ganada I do not see why you should not apply it to every part of Canada. I do not think it is a proper principle. I think ,we may frame a clause which will get around the difficulty as respects Ontario, by assuming that at a certain stage these lists are provincial lists, prepared under this provincial Act. But I would insist, for my part, that the whole machinery of section 32 be the machinery employed for the revision; I believe it is the only satisfactory machinery we can get. It is going to cost some money, but I believe it will give us as nearly perfect a voters' list as we have ever had in this country.

In the cities of Montreal, Quebec, Three Rivers, Sherbrooke, St. Hya-cinthe, Hull and Valleyfield, the lists are revised every two years; in rural municipalities in the province of Quebec they are revised every year between September and November. These lists, I understand, are to be taken as a basis. They are to be handed to whatever officer is appointed to deal with them, and to these lists will be added the names of those who should go on, and from them will be struck off the names of those who, it is claimed, are not entitled to vote. But these lists, I understand, shall be the basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: When the matter was up before, my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) stated to me, I think, publicly, the fact that if we made this two years, he saw no objection. We are making it two years, to make it conform.
I was absent when this matter came up and I wanted to make sure.

As regards the Ontario situation, there is very little difference between the view of the minister (Mr. Guthrie) and that of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). As I understand the situation, if the Provincial Government has adopted certain lists, those lists shall be accepted by the Dominion for two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As a basis.

As a basis. Then, the succeeding years have been the source of difference, the leader of the Opposition contending that for succeeding lists, if there should be a Dominion election, the Ontario lists that may be considered to be lists in course of preparation for provincial elections, lists prepared by the assessors of the municipalities, might be accepted as a basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If they have been revised by the judge.

Yes. I understood the minister to say that he is willing to accept those lists with the idea that they are provincial lists in course of preparation. Then, the matter becomes just one of how those lists shall be finally revised. I was going to make this suggestion with a view to save expense, that instead, at that point, of appointing a large number of enumerators, say, one in each polling subdivision, to revise those lists, the provincial idea be adopted of having a Board of Revision for the whole riding. I would just add this in reply to what the minister said. He spoke of the lists prepared by the assessors as "half-baked" lists. I think he will find that those lists will be very complete, for this reason: the minister stated that the assessors are not particularly concerned to put on the list anybody except those who are municipal voters. In the last session of the Ontario Legislature, I think I am right in saying that a law was passed removing the property qualification entirely in municipal elections, and that means that the municipal franchise becomes manhood and womanhood franchise. Therefore, the municipal lists will correspond almost exactly with the provincial voters' lists or the Dominion voters' lists, so that very little revision would be necessary, and I believe a Board of Revision, such as is contemplated under the Ontario Act, would be very suitable for Dominion purposes also. If the minister could accept that suggestion, the whole question might be very well agreed upon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Would one
registrar for each municipality not be sufficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think that would be sufficient. I do not think he could possibly do the work in the time allotted. Unless we consider that this has been drawn with the idea of making half a dozen periods of time fit in and dovetail, the thing is going to be thrown out of joint. You must have regard to the amount of work that has to be done in a very limited period of time. The very least you can get on with is one



registrar to a polling subdivision. While it may be that in a compact little polling division in some little township one registrar could do mor'e than the work required of him in that subdivision, one hon. member pointed out to me just a moment ago that in the West we may have to get two or three registrars in some subdivisions to do this little bit of work. That is the difficulty.	*

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would it be possible, as it is now six o'clock, to have an amendment -drafted before eight o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As long as it is a provincial list in course of preparation where it has reached the stage where a judge has revised it, but has not been finally revised, because-* the final revision would not take place until just before a provincial election, a provincial list in course of preparation in Ontario might be adopted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As regards revision by a judge, assuming there were no appeals to a judge, as long as the formalities of the law had been complied with, that section of the Act would then be regarded as having been complied with.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I should like to see the amendment before I say anything.

Hundreds of names might still be subject to revision by the judge.
