speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at six o'clock we were discussing section 32 with special reference to the province of Ontario and the peculiar situation which has arisen in that province by reason of an Act, passed during its last session by the legislature of Ontario, known as the Election Laws Amendment Act. I make this statement so that the committee may understand the situation. That Act provided for the making of voters' lists for both municipal and provincial purposes. By the terms of the Act the list is specifically a provincial voters' list, but I think that a strict reading of the Act shows that there would be no provincial voters' lists prepared and completed unless a provincial election were held. Section 25 of the Act referred to provides:
The list so prepared shall be subject to revision by the judge of the Country Court and shall be dealt with in all respects in the man-

ner provided by The Ontario Voters' Lists Act. and the last list prepared for any municipality and finally revised by the judge shall be the proper list to be used at any election to the Assembly held before another list has been prepared and revised as herein provided, but whenever an election to the Assembly is to be held the lists shall be subject to further revision, as hereinafter provided, as to persons entitled or claiming to be entitled to be entered thereon as qualified to vote at elections to the Assembly and as to persons entered thereon who are not qualified to vote at elections to the Assembly.
The position is this:	We have in Ontario a list of voters for provincial purposes which was used in October last. Under the language of section 32 of the present Bill as we propose to amend it that would be the list for the next two years. It would form the basis of the Dominion list should a Dominion election be held within the next two years. But in the province of Ontario it is not likely that there will be a new provincial list until there is a new provincial election, and we cannot fix a date in regard to that event. It is a contingency. Now, my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) and the leader of the Opposition propose that we should adopt what are practically municipal lists of the province of Ontario as a basis for Dominion voters' lists. I object to that; if you do it in Ontario you might as well do it in the other provinces. My view is that the Dominion Government should disregard municipal lists and franchises and prepare Dominion lists upon a uniform basis, having general application throughout all provinces. To meet the difficulty I would be prepared to go thus far, namely, that when a general election is called, if there be no provincial voters' lists in Ontario which would be available-of course for two years we shall have it-then, that a list which is in course of preparation as a provincial list, and which has gone so far as to be finally revised by a county judge, should form the basis for Dominion purposes. There would be the same power to revise that list, to add to or subtract from it, as there would be in regard to any other provincial list which was adopted as a basis for Dominion lists under section 32. I make this suggestion only as a compromise, it is to meet the peculiar case of the province of Ontario. But if the principle of this exception is to be extended throughout Canada I will not agree to it; I would far rather have the clause as drawn. If it meets the objections of my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition, as he voiced them this afternoon, I would be prepared, owing to the peculiar nature of the Ontario

legislation upon this subject, to go as far as I have intimated. There will also be some minor amendments, in addition to this, to correct some clerical errors; and there will have to be some formal amendments to make the section workable.
I would put in a special provision in section 32 as follows:
Provided that in and for the province of Ontario, if there he no provincial voters' lists which have been prepared and completed within two years immediately preceding the issue of the writ, provincial voters' lists in course of preparation under the Elections Laws Amendment Act, 1920 of the said province, which have been finally revised by the county judge under section twenty eight of the said Act, shall be adopted under this section for the said province, but the same shall be subject to all the provisions of this section as to additions thereto and subtractions therefrom as in the case of provincial lists prepared and completed for provincial purposes.
I am not moving this as an amendment now, but I am offering it as a suggestion to see if we can settle our difficulties. If my hon. friends see fit to adopt it I think we can work it out.
Suppose at the next session of the provincial legislature there should be an amendment to that section of the law to which reference is made, how would it affect the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It would affect the situation very materially and might necessitate an amendment to meet that new condition.
Why should we have to depend on any authority other than this Parliament for the right to have our own franchise Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I agree that this House should be able to decide upon its own franchise Act, but it is a very difficult problem in a country like this, with nine provinces each having different election laws. It is a task of very great difficulty. Here we have a difficulty and we are trying by a method of compromise to overcome it. 1 think this may be done without interfering with the principle upon which the Bill is framed, and if it is a satisfactory compromise it may get us over some of our difficulties.

Is there a provision in
the Provincial Voters' List Act for the revision of the municipal lists by the county judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, the ordinary revision takes place every year before the county judge and the lists would be avail-247*
able to the extent that they had been finally revised by the county judge.

I am afraid that in almost every electoral district, when we come to the Dominion elections, we will find a varied condition; that some municipal lists for a particular year, say, will have been revised before the county judge while others will not have been so revised, necessitating the use of this year's lists in one municipality and last year's list in another municipality as the basis. It will create a great deal of confusion.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think any great confusion will arise on that account. I thought of that. It would merely mean that in the municipalities where they were finally revised they would be the basis while in the municipalities where they were not finally revised they would not be the basis and the enumerator would make the revision.

It seems to me that logically the system of franchise which a province had created for itself is the system which we ought to adopt for that province. To use a legal phrase, if we adopt the franchise system of the province, that province is estopped from criticising that action on our part. But there was one suggestion which was made, and somewhat dwelt upon by the leader of the Opposition, and that was that in rural subdivisions, or municipalities-subdivisions particularly- if a man finds himself cut off the voters' list when he should be on, he can go into a polling booth, swear that he is entitled to vote, and be allowed to vote. I have as much faith in humanity as probably anybody; I also have some experience, and perhaps I have some common sense; but if anybody thinks that in some townships I know of-they are not in my county-oh, no-that it is perfectly all right to leave an arrangement like that wide open, he has another think coming. What is to prevent people being injected in, say from the West and making false statements?-and people frequently treat it as a joke when it comes to cheating the franchise and the customs. If you have men and women coming in and making these statements, in a close constituency it will turn the election. If you look for them after the deed is done you cannot find them. It is easy. If the vote is to be allowed without any further presumption than that established by the readiness of the party applying to take his oath, the door is wide open for fraud, and certainly in some constituencies and at

some times I know that would be a mild dose of fraud for some people to take. I would sincerely ask the leader of the Opposition to reconsider that idea and to give us something a little more guarded.

The minister has stated
that in case the province of Ontario should pass legislation amending their present law it might be inconvenient and would render an amendment to our Act necessary. That being so I would suggest thalt the minister consider the advisability of providing a further amendment somewhat along these lines: Provided further that in case such Provincial Government have passed an amendment to their present franchise law which would render the amendment which the minister now submits inoperative, section 23 stand as it is to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The amendment, in the way it is drawn, is intended Ito cover that. Just as soon as there is a provincial list prepared and completed for provincial purposes, that is the list. If the Ontario Government should see fit Ito change its law, or should hold an election on that provincial voters' list, the proposed amendment has no force or effect.

I would like to ask the minister what he meant when he said, in reply to the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), that if the provincial legislature made an amendment to Itheir present franchise law it would necessitate the further amendment of this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If they amend it so
as to change sedtion 28 in such a way that there would be no revision before a county judge, we would have to amend our Act.
Then let us amend this section to provide that if they do make such an amendment to Itheir Act the present section stands as it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think it would be
simpler to amend our law later than to amend it nowr.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As I understand the suggestion the minister has made, it meets, to a certain extent, one of the main points we have raised, namely, avoiding duplication and expense in the preparation of lists. As his suggestion reads, the lists which are now prepared and which are the lists used at the last provincial elections Will be the basis of the lists for the next federal election until a period of two years has expired. There may be certain changes to make, certain additions 
to and subtractions from the provincial
lists. Thereafter lists that have been made up, to the extent to which they have been made up and revised before the Court of Revision shall be available for use for federal purposes. So far there is a saving in the expense of the enumeration of a very large number of names, but there is left to the Government the revision of the list by officers appointed by themselves. While the Government does not meet us on the latter point, we preferring to have no enumerators or registrars appointed but to have the revision made by established judicial bodies, nevertheless the proposal does meet us to the extent I have indicated and as such will be welcomed, and I thank my hon. friend for. it.

But the appeal to the
judge remains?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. Then, if we have got over that point, there are quite a number of other amendments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand the minister desires to move this as an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Assume that
the Ontario law was in effect this year and that the new lists were prepared in the spring of next year and revised by the judge in the summer, would such Ontario lists be used after the revision had been made by the judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It would only be where there are no provincial lists prepared and completed in the two years, which would mean the following year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What I would like to say to my hon. friend is, that his . suggestion would be still more agreeable if those lists could be used just as soon as they were ready.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I could not do that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like to put that suggestion on record at any rate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move to amend line22 of page 14 of the Bill by striking out "one year" and inserting "two years."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move to amend line 33 of page 14 of the Bill by striking out "Schedules A and B respectively," and inserting ''Schedule A."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move this amendment:
In line 9 of page 15 of the Bill strike out "Schedules" and insert "Schedule", and in line 10 strike out "and B" and insert "for urban polling divisions", and also in line 10 after "section" insert "and the returning officer for rural polling divisions, respectively".
The reason for that is this: In the urban polling divisions the registrar is the man to do it, and in the rural polling divisions the returning officer, that is where the voters' lists do not conform.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I now beg leave to
move the following amendment:
In Schedule A on pageg 16 of the Bill strike out rule 1 and insert the following:
"Rule 1.-Immediately after the receipt of the WTit the returning officer shall appoint, hy writing, in Form E one person only to be registrar of voters in each city, town or incorporated village which is wholly or partly contained in the electoral district for which the election is pending and which has a population of over 1,000 or less than 4,000 persons, and one for each additional 4,000 persons, who shall, before acting as such, take the oath in Form F; and the registrars so appointed shall be assigned by the returning officer to such parts or such number of polls as he may deem right and proper."
In the section as drawn there was a discretion, which was indefinite, as to how many registrars would be appointed. In the amendment which I have proposed there is one registrar for a population of from one thousand to four thousand, and an additional registrar for each four thousand persons. I think it is better to .make the provision definite rather than to leave it discretionary.

I was not able to be
here this afternoon. Will my hon. friend tell me what conclusion has been reached with respect to the arrangement that was made about the Nova Scotia lists, and to some extent the New Brunswick lists also? We had come to an understanding with the hon. gentleman concerning the Nova Scotia lists. What I desire to know is whether that arrangement is being carried out.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Well, we came to a tentative understanding I agree; but if my hon. friend was in the House on the 18th and 19th of May, when the discussion on our proposals took place, I think he must have come to the conclusion that we had only agreed to disagree. As I announced this afternoon, under the circumstances we could not go further with the proposal which that conference or committee decided upon, and I have resolved on behalf of the Government to proceed with the Bill as drawn. However, during the course of this afternoon, we have come to some other conclusions in regard to the voters' lists in the province of Ontario, and I assumed that they would probably settle our difficulty- at all events, very largely.
At the discussion which took place after the conference-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will pardon me, but will he allow the committee to adopt the amendment to rule, which was proposed a few minutes ago. Shall the amendment carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to. i

At the discussion that took place after the conference referred to there was no question raised with regard to the Nova Scotia lists. There was some discussion regarding the Ontario lists and municipal lists, but the assent-the agreement if we may call it so-that had been reached at the conference affecting the Nova Scotia lists was not the subject of any dissension later on, and I have,, up to this moment, assumed that that agreement- again I say, if we may call it agreement- was to be carried out. The essential point of difference was this: I had proposed an amendment to the effect that the lists of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick prepared for provincial purposes should be accepted as final. My hon. friend said they could not agree to that, but they would agree to this. That the lists should be accepted as final, subject to two qualifications; first, that in the urban districts the right of appeal to the county judge should remain-to which I had no objection; and second, that as to the other districts it should be agreed that we should grant the right of a man to swear his name on the list on the day of election in the presence of two witnesses, who would certify that he was qualified to vote-to which, although I thought it an unnecessary cog in the machine, I offered no objection. There was no difference of opinion in the end between my hon. friend and myself. All he desired in regard to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-although I speak particularly of Nova Scotia-I was content to accept, and I am astonished to be told to-day that that agreement is not to be carried out.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know on what assumption, my hon. friend thought we were binding the House of Commons by our conference. We certainly sought to reach a basis of agreement; that was the

purpose of the conference; and so far as those who were in immediate attendance at the conference are concerned, I think they were all fairly well satisfied with the proposals then made. But when the matter came before the House of Commons I certainly found otherwise. Whether it was in regard particularly to Nova Scotia or to some of the other provinces I do not say at the moment, but I know there was general dissatisfaction, and I have since learned that on this side of the House, particularly in regard to Nova .Scotia, the proposals were not suitable to those gentlemen on this side who sit for constituencies in that province. Under these circumstances I would not ask the House to consider any suggestions of mine as constituting a binding agreement, and I so notified the House this afternoon when I brought the amendments forward. I thought at the time that they offered a fair solution of our troubles, but other people took a different view. The conclusion of the Government was, and is, that under all the circumstances it is better to proceed with the clause as originally drafted.
Mr. FI'BLDING: I quite agree with my hon. friend that neither of us can bind the House of Commons, hut I thought in view of what had occurred at the conference that if he on the one side and I on the other agreed that probably there would be no difficulty in obtaining the assent of the House of Commons. If my hon. friend found any dissent in respect to the treatment of Nova Scotia he did not find it from any discussion that occurred in this House; he must have found it in some other way as to which he has not taken this House into his confidence. The point of difference was that the hon. gentleman in his original proposal desired to appoint a number of so-called enumerators or registrars, who would have the right to put on additional names. I tried to point out to the House, and I think I persuaded the hon. gentleman, that that was a needless waste of public money. I say that the lists of Nova Scotia are fairly and properly made, and if taken as final no harm would be done. But as my hon. friend said we were to have a reference to the county judge in urban districts, I had no objection; and, although I think it is unnecessary to have men coming to the poll on election day with two brother electors and swearing themselves on, I have not objected to it. But I have objected to the power of the Government to appoint an

army of enumerators for the special purpose of putting on names which they could not put on in any other way. I do not want to argue this further, because it is so absolutely monstrous that I am astonished at the attitude of the hon. gentleman.

May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) why he makes that statement? That statement does not apply to the province of Ontario; and is the province of Nova Scotia a great deal worse than the province of Ontario? In the province of Ontario we are accustomed, until a man is proved a rascal, to consider him as an ordinary fair-minded human being. I do not presume to lecture a man ,so much older than I am, but this business af forever casting mud oveir everything before it is proved there is any wrong, is destroying this country. I do not think that a man so great in the annals of this country, and so patriotic, as my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) should engage in it,, because he of all men has set the rest of this country an extremely bad example in that respect.

I have not presumed to discuss the lists of Ontario, because I confess that I am not familiar with those lists. It would be a good thing if we could have a uniform system in all parts of Canada in regard to the lists, but inasmuch as different rules prevail in the various provinces, it has been found necessary to vary the provision even under this law. The whole story is a very simple one. We have lists prepared every year in Nova Scotia for provincial elections. They are prepared by no political authority; they are prepared by municipal councils. There is a right of appeal to the sheriff. There has been no evidence to show that that right of appeal has ever been improperly used; in fact, there have been few, if any, appeals. The hon. .minister was willing to have these lists taken .as final, subject to these two conditions: that in the case of the urban districts there should be appeal to the county judge,-as to which I took the ground that while I thought it was unnecessary, still I had no objection to that appeal;-and, second, that if a man was left off the list he ought to have the right to come to the polling station on election day and be allowed to swear himself on again. I said that although I thought it was not necessary I had no objection to that. What I did object to, and what I object to now, and what I am obliged to continue to object to, is the right of the

Government to appoint an army of so-called enumerators or registrars through a partisan returning officer for no other purpose than to make partisan lists, although we were told this to be a fair, a just and a generous Bill.
Amendment to rule 1 agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
On page 17, Mr. Chairman, some change has to be made. I therefore move to amend Schedule A on page 17 of the Bill by adding at the end of Rule 2 the following words, " and such notice shall be so posted at least four days before the first day of registration."
And also by adding thereafter the following paragraph:
He shall also, before nine o'clock of the first day fixed for the registration of voters, cause at least five copies of such notice to be posted up in some conspicuous place outside of and near to the place where he sits for the registration of voters, and he shall see that these notices remain duly posted up thoughout the whole period of registration.
It is to give the public notice that the registrar is sitting there.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Then, Mr. Chairman,
I beg to move to amend Rule 3 in Schedule A by adding after the word "registrar" the words "and additional registrar," and by striking from lines 1 and 2, the words "city, town, or incorporated village or part thereof" and inserting in line 1 after the words "within the" the words "territorial limit for which he is appointed."
I would like to have the section read as amended so that we can understand it. The minister is introducing many amendments and hon. members have no information as Ito what the amendments mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition has a copy of these amendments. The section will now read:
Every registrar and additional registrar shall provide within the territorial limit for which he is appointed, a convenient place, properly lighted and heated, and being the place mentioned in such notice ;-
And so on.

That
means that there will be a registrar in every polling distridt?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There is power in cases of cities to appoint sufficient registrars for every 4,000 of the population. If the population is from 1,000 to 4,000 there shall be one registrar, and for every additional 4,000
an additional registrar. This imposes on both the registrar and the additional registrar the duty of having these premises property lighted and heated and of giving Ithe proper notice for the holding of the sitting.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have as.-
sumed that it would expedite matters to have the minister bring forward all his amendments and have them passed as read, on the understanding that we would havp a chance to consider the whole section as amended before we>
finally pass on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We can take them all
and then we can have the Chairman read the clauses over. The amendments are all more or less technical; they do not go to the principle or the root of the matter. The other amendments are as follows:
In schedule A, rule 4, paragraph (b), strike out in the fifth and sixth lines the words "and proper polling division." Insert before the word "address" in line 5, the word "and." Strike out in the sixth and seventh lines the words "on the registrar's preliminary, or compilation, list " and insert " in an index book which shall be kept for each polling division in form K6 Ito this Act." In the last two lines of paragraph (b) of rule 4 strike out "on such preliminary list" and insert " in such index book." We are providing that each registrar shall have a proper index book in which the registrations may be enltered as they come in, and Ithat such book shall be alphabetically indexed and convenient of reference. When the Bill was first prepared the use of such a book was not contemplated, but Mr. Castonguay says that it is indispensable Ito have an index book for quick reference, and it is to comply with his suggestion that these amendments are necessary.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendments agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: On the last line of page 17, the word "or" before Ithe word "town" should be struck out, and after the word "town" the words "or incorporated village" should be added.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speechtext:
In schedule A, rule 6,
line 2, strike out "two" and inserlt "three." It is thought that' two days is too short a time within which Ito get these lists out. Then, in paragraph (a), first line, strike out "preliminary or compilation list" and insert "index book." In line 7, paragraph (a), after the words "according to," insert

"the first letter of the surnames.' In line 11 of paragraph (a) strike out "preliminary or compilation list" and insert "index book."
I would suggest an amendment to meet the question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) this afternoon. At the end of paragraph (a) insert the following words:
The name of a married woman or a widow shall be entered on the index book under the first letter of the surname of her husband or deceased husband, respectively.
In paragraph (b), line 2, add the word "incorporated" before the word "village," and in paragraph (c), second line, after the word "candidates" add the words "upon nomination day."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendments agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move to amend
schedule A rule (8) by striking out in the fourth and fifth lines the word "a certified copy of the list prepared by him" and inserting the words "the index book kept by him for each polling division under his *jurisdiction."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As regards schedule A rule (11), a difficulty arises that, in Nova Scotia, and also I think in New Brunswick, *there are no junior or senior county court judges; there are just county court judges. It has been drawn to my attention that this rule will not suit Nova Scotia nor New Brunswick. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I also move to amend schedule A, rule (11) by striking out the word "he" in line 24, and inserting the words "each revising officer." This says: "He shall appoint a clerk." It should read: "Each revising officer shall appoint a clerk."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move to amend schedule A, rule (14), paragraph (d), by striking out in line 8 the word "or" where it first occurs and after the word "town" inserting the words "or incorporated village" to make this read: "city, town or incorporated village." It reads now: "city or town."

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
CMr. Guthrie.]

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I also move to amend schedule A, rule (14), paragraph (d), by striking out in line 9 the word "part" and inserting the word "section," and in the last line before the word "such" by inserting the word "any." The paragraph reads: "in this part"; it should read: "in this section." speechtext: I move to amend schedule A, rule (16), by striking out in the third line the word "making" and inserting the words "and make all," and in line 5 by striking out the word "certifying" and inserting the words "shall certify," and in line 6 by striking out the word "dispatch" and inserting the words "shall dispatch by registered mail." speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
In rule 17, I think, if possible at all, the minister should make the time longer than four days prior to an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
When we get these changes made, we can read the section and then suggestions or amendments may be made. As regards Rule 17, in the computation of time between the final revision of an urban list, that is, a list for a city, town or village, and the date of handing the list to the candidate, a period of only eight days has been allowed. It has been pointed out that a strike may occur in a printing or newspaper officer or other unavoidable delays may take place and for some reason or another the lists may not be printed within those eight days. The King's Printer pointed out this difficulty, and he suggested this amendment which I will move because I think we should make some provision. It is just to provide for unforeseen accidents or delays. I move that schedule A, rule (17), be amended by adding at the end of the rule the following paragraph:

Provided, however, that if the revising officer shall report to the Chief Electoral Officer that the lists cannot be printed in time for delivery to the candidates as required by this Rule, the Chief Electoral Officer may order that the printing of the lists he dispensed with; and in such case the revising officer shall cause to he made for each candidate one complete copy of the list as finally revised and certified under his hand as a true copy and he shall deliver or send by registered mail to each candidate or to his agent one copy of such list at least four days before the polling day.
Candidates, although they may not have their lists actually certified, printed and complete, will, I think, in every case have lists; but allowing eight days for printing the lists will allow only four clear days before polling day for possession of the printed list. There is no doubt they will have preliminary lists, but they will not have all the corrections. The usual experience, of course, is that candidates are represented on appeals and they will know what changes are made. It would be better if we had longer than four days for printed lists, but allowing every day we can, four days is all we can allow.
It is very short.
In my election I did not get some of the lists nor a copy of any kind until four days after the election was over.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That was a great misfortune. We are trying to remedy that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
These are not the rural
lists.
Mr. 'CALDWELL: What governs the rural lists ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The rural list is not
printed at all ; it is delivered fourteen days before-not later than nomination day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt this discussion, but I undestand there is an agreement between the Acting Solicitor General and the loader of the Opposition- which will undoubtedly be confirmed by
the unanimous consent of the com-
9	p.m. mittee,-that, instead of discussing
these amendments as we reach them, the minister be allowed to move all these amendments; that they be adopted for the time being, and then that the committee go over the rules as amended, reserving to members of the committee the right to move at that time any further amendments they may deem advisable.

speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Mr. GUTHRIE' The draftsman of this Bill thought that was a necessary provision because circumstances might arise where, in the opinion of the Chief Electoral Officer, it .might be more judicious and less expensive if the lists were revised by enumeration instead of registration. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am as strongly opposed to the whole system of enumeration as it is possible to be. Unless some other member of the committee sees any wisdom in retaining it I move to strike it out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause as amended carry?

Before
the clause carries, I would point out that provision was made in it for transferring voters from one polling division to another. I would like to understand at what time that transfer can be made. Can it be made after a copy of the list is given to the candidates, or must it be made prior to that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No. I think that has to be done under section 28, an earlier section than this. The polling divisions are arranged under section 28, but it is quite possible that a Dominion polling division and a local polling division may not be co-extensive, and in order to make the provincial polling divisions conform for Dominion purposes some names may have to be transferred from one division to another. That duty so far as the urban divisions are concerned is to be performed by the registrar, and in the rural divisions by the returning officer. It is merely for putting them in an appropriate Dominion polling division. That must certainly be done before the registrar, in the urban case, and the enumerator, in the rural case, certifies and delivers his lists to the returning officer.

I venture to say, Mr. Chairman, that every period of time that

is given in connection with this section for the taking of an election is too short- absolutely too short. In our province the lists are prepared on the 5th day of April each year. The electoral list is an old friend to everybody in our province; they know all about it. Here is a condition brought about where we do not see the electoral list till the morning of the election day. A candidate*is rarely at home in his own place on election day, and the result will be that he will not see the electoral list at all. I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that this is a most extraordinary piece of machinery. We hear a great deal of the War-time Elections Act as being a black mark on the good life of this country; but let me assure you, Sir, that although fair promises were made at the start in the case of this Bill, yet if it were possible for any thing to be worse than the War-time Elections Act, this Bill can be so characterized. The minister could not take any more to himself than he is doing. He is preparing the list himself, appointing his own officers; everything about it from stem to stern, lock, stock and barrel, is his own creation, without one scintilla of independence in the election from start to finish. That is the kind of election we are going to have when the time comes. The only consolation is that if the Canadian people are aroused, as I hope they will be, to the real situation of this country no machinery of the minister no matter how water-tight it may be will suffice. There will be enough independence in Canada to hurl the minister and his ministry, and everything belonging to him, _ clean over the bank, and get back to a condition where the people can once more breathe freely in this country. Then they will be rid of Unionist Government, and rid of the machinery that the Unionist Government has created. Then we shall once more get back to the state where the people will be able to go up to the polls and freely express their opinion. We have not got that situation to-day; and the minister, the Prime Minister, and every other member of the Government, need not be surprised that there is disorder, dissatisfaction and unrest abroad, and that disbelief in every institution of this country prevails generally. How can it be otherwise when in the hot days of the summer we are sitting down to manufacture such a law as this for the Canadian people-a law manufactured with the hope that the people will have nothing to say about how they shall be governed, or what laws shall be enacted-nothing but the black machinery called into existence by the
minister, something like what I hear is in operation on the adjoining racetrack, a sort of automatic machine. That is the sort of machine we are going to have rather than a fair election, lit is something under which nobody will have anything to say, something that is created by the will of the minister for the ministry and for their own purposes. I would certainly say there is no use putting forth any amending proposition, no use at all. The minister got into a reasonable frame of mind a couple of weeks ago. At any rate he said he was getting reasonable. He declare that he was going to accept our lists in Nova Scotia, that he was going to be equally reasonable in a number of things; but whether he invited the crack of the whip or not he got it and he came down from the tree quicker than any coon in the world ever did. Now he is right back where he was before. He simply told his followers, "Pray, gentlemen, foTgive me. In a moment of weakness I was falling back on something that was less drastic than what you put before me. I will take it all back, and this will go through, if possible, in a form seven times worse than it was before". That is the situation that we have now. Surely there are hon. gentlemen opposite who believe that presenting a man with an electoral list on election day is not a fair proposition. The returning officer does not see it; nobody sees it; nobody knows whose name is on it; and the good, honest man, who sits supporting the Government, says: "No, you will not see the list. We are going to pass it to returning officer at some time before six o'clock in the morning, and you may have the privi-ledge of seeing it some time after the election is over". Hon. gentlemen opposite come from different parts of the country. They pride themselves on their fairness and on their honesty in everything else except an election, but when it comes to an election there is apparently no desire for fair dealing at all. The only satisfaction, Mr. Chairman, is this: I feel confident, as far as my province is concerned, that no machinery the minister can devise can bring him any other result but the one round robin that he will get from that province.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if we are not making further amendments to thie clause it is simply because we had a conference this afternoon, when some slight change was agreed to which made the clause a little less objectionable. I would not, however, like the minister or the Government to think that the clause as it

stands is at all acceptable. If it carries, it carries on division.

Before the clause is finally disposed of, I would like to call attention to the fact that the French copy which has been supplied to members does not give any definition in the interpretation clause of the terms "urban polling division" and "rural polling division." I merely rise for the purpose of calling attention to the oversight so that whoever is responsible for it will correct it when the time comes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I will see that the
necessary correction is made. These changes were put in very early in the discussion, before the Bill was produced for second reading, and I cannot understand why they were omitted from the French translation.

The
provisions of this clause to my mind settle the partisan character of this measure. In plain language it provides that a partisan returning officer has the power to appoint other partisans in every polling division for the purpose of making the lists. These officers are not selected by judges. They are selected by the Government. The Government wiE select one of their own supporters, and the chances are that they will select a man nominated by the candidate whom they intend to run in the district. That candidate will then submit the names of the registrars in the various districts. So that, as my friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) says, the whole section from first to last is most unfair and most objectionable. It is worse than the old system of partisan revising barristers which existed from 1885 to 1807. Under that system we had a partisan, it is true, but he was a man of some standing in the community, and he took the responsibility of making the lists. He did not appoint a lot of heelers to make the list; he made it himself and took the full responsibility. That system was found to work very badly indeed, but it is not nearly so bad nor so unfair as the proposed system because we have not one man only to do the work but fifty or sixty men, all off a partisan character, and each doing his own small part of the work in the various districts. The Liberal party made strong objection to the old system which provided for the appointment of revising barristers, and in the platform of the Liberal party in the election of 1896 provision was made for its repeal and a return to something like a 
fair electoral law. The Liberal party carried out their promise and in 1897 the practice was abolished and we returned to what has ever since been recognized as a fair system. The only three occasions in the history of the Dominion on which an attempt has been made to gain a partisan advantage from the election law, were, I am glad to say, made by the party represented by hon. gentlemen opposite. The first attempt was made in 1882 when the Gerrymander Act was passed, which is remembered as one of the darkest blots on the record of the Conservative party; the next attempt was made in 1886, when partisan revising barristers were provided for; and now we have the third attempt. I am glad to -say that the history of the Liberal party is free from any such offence.
The clause retains some very objectionable features, but that is the main one,- that the Government are selecting the jury to try themselves. That is what it comes to. But I wish to warn hon. gentlemen opposite that they will not always be on the Treasury benches. When an opportunity is given to the people to express their views at the polls, this Government, in my opinion, will be defeated, and then hon. gentlemen opposite will have to move over to this side of the House, and they will not always find the Liberal party so magnanimous as they were in 1897. I want to say to hon. gentlemen opposite that they are to-day building up a system that they themselves will have to meet a little later on. I think it is in the Psalms of David where a man is described as digging a pit in which he is himself to fall. My hon. friends are putting up a stone wall to knock their own heads against in future; and they will find that the law they are passing to-day will operate against them so that they may be kept out of power for a very long time. Therefore I do not want to let this opportunity pass without giving them warning.
There is nothing fair about this law. These partisan registrars are not appointed by judges as was proposed, and it would be impossible to make a law that would be more unfair. There is no use discussing this further, for our objections have been placed before the minister over and over again. The old feature that we complained of at the start still continues in this section ;we have tried to remedy it; but it appears that no concession is to be made and that the partisan character of the officers who make the lists is still to be maintained.

I would like to correct
the impression I gave to the committee regarding the Franch translation. The reason for my error is that in the English copy the definition of the rural and urban polling divisions are set out under the letters (v) and (w), while in the French copy they come under letters (c) and (d).

On Rule 3-Revision of lists; attendance of registrar:

Why should a registrar in the rural district be called upon to be in his place only in the afternoon? In the urban district he has to be there all day, why should he not be in his office in the rural district all day?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is considered that in a rural division there will be from 300 to 350 all told, and by being in his office for five or six hours a day he can hear all the complaints. It is thought that this will be a satisfactory time to meet the convenience of all parties. If we are going to have him attend for longer hours, I fancy he will want more money.

A man in the country would take very much longer to do the work. He is not an expert such as you usually find in a city or town. A man in the country as a rule wilj not be accustomed to this kind of work and he will be much longer at it than the expert city man. I think the time is too short.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am told that the experience in Saskatchewan is that as a rule there are not five appeals in any rural division. I think that from five to ten would be probably the limit in the older-settled portions of Ontario. I am satisfied that in the county in which I live every man in a rural division knows every other man, and I do not think'there will be many appeals. There will be some.
I understood this to be for the making of the lists.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This is after the list is made up. People may object and ask to have the list corrected, and for the purpose of hearing objections and taking the proper action he shall sit for five or six hours a day.
When does he settle down to prepare the list?

speechtext:

On Rule 4-addition and elimination of names; correction of errors:

This rule is very objectionable. It enables the registrar to strike a name off the list after the list has been completed and handed to the candidate on nomination day. He can keep the list for five days after nomination, because it may be done any time up to the tenth day before election, and during those five days he can strike the names of opponents from the lists that have been given to the candidates. This section is so objectionable that I should not think the minister would want to retain it. Fifteen days before the election the electoral list is supposed to be completed, and is delivered to the candidate, and that ought to be final. There is no reason why names should be struck from the list after that date. There may be a reason why names omitted should be added, but there certainly cannot be any reason why names should be struck from the list without notice. You will observe that the registrar can, without any notice to the voter, the candidate or any other person, go behind his door in his own house and privately put his pen through the name of a man who has been regularly placed on the list. That is what it means. It puts a power in the hands of the partisan registrar to disfigure the list and change it after it has been settled. I do not think the minister should ask us to pass this section. It was so objectionable that one of his own supporters protested against it a few days ago. I do not think that any fair man should say that the registrar should have the right to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend

The registrar makes his list and signs it on the fifteenth day before polling and no later than nomination day he delivers a copy of that list to the candidate. Then for five days thereafter he sits at this place which he designates to hear complaints. That would bring it to the tenth day before polling, and during

In like manner, if he is satisfied that the name has been improperly put on by himself, he may remove it. I think it was properly drawn in the first place. I misapprehended the objection of my hon. friend, and 'I think he misapprehended the rule, although I took it for granted he was right. I will have to move the reconsideration of rule 4, as I misapprehended the objection of my hon. friend.

Under the provision as it stands I could go to the registrar and say: John Smith is not entitled to vote, and in support of that statement I could give the most trivial reason; the registrar thereupon has it absolutely, in his power to strike that name off the list. speechtext:
I may point out to the hon. gentleman as indicative of our expressed intention upon that subject that the corresponding section of the British Act gives power absolutely to the Secretary of State without the intervention of His Majesty in council at all. But, inasmuch as we have the liberty to designate what authority within this country shall exercise different powers, Parliament wisely decided that this power should be vested in the Governor in Council, not in any one minister and it is the Governor in Council that requires to be satisfied. In three out of five cases of revocation it is the	duty of	the	Secretary
of State to give notice to the party concerned so that he may have an inquiry. lit will always be in the power of the Governor in 'Council, if it is of opinion that enquiry is necessary and the Secretary of State has reported without inquiry, to refer the report back' until inquiry is made, so that the parties concerned will have the full protection of the Governor in Council.
iMr. EULER: I understood the minister to say that the reason he could not place in the same category as the the others this particular clause whereby the person whose certificate is to be cancelled has the right to a hearing before a judge, was that it would destroy uniformtiy so far as the British Act is concerned. I understand the minister to state now that the British Act is not the same as ours with respect to these clauses which give to the people the right under certain circumstances to be tried before a judge. I would suggest under the circumstances that we might also place this clause in the category of the others. I 
think the principle would be absolutely right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
misunderstood me. I said in regard to what authority exercises the powers of granting certificates or of revoking them, we might have designated the Governor in Council or the Secretary of State. There is no need for uniformity in that regard; and if we thought it desirable I am not prepared to say that we could not provide for inquiry in all these cases. But even though it be our opinion that it would be better to do that-in other words, that the British Parliament did not go far enough-I called the attention of the House" to the undesirability of our proceeding by making differences unless they are really of major importance and cannot possibly wait for consultation. But if we get away from dealing only with matters concerning which there has been consultation, sooner or later one of the Parliaments concerned will find itself perhaps unconsciously outside of the uniformity. As I say, the British Parliament was scrupulously careful not to enact anything that would be necessary to the general Imperial naturalization without previous consultation with the Dominions. I think that -we owe them the courtesy of following that example, even though w^e may adhere, perhaps, a trifle more than is absolutely necessary to uniformity in our provisions. I would not like by this Bill, which was introduced largely for the purpose of clearing away a misunderstanding, to start out to make a general improvement of existing law. I do think that there is room for improvement; if I continue to have any responsibility in connection with the matter, there are suggestions which it seems to me might very properly be made. As I have said, the minister charged with the Bill of 1918 when it went through the Imperial House observed, with regard to different suggestions that came from members there,' that he thought- they would form a proper subject of consultation in the future.

If subsection (b) on page 2 is an old section I have nothing to say about it, but if it is new I think it is rather severe. It mentions a term of penal servitude; that might be a month in jail or it might he a fortnight, I suppose.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I understand it, penal servitude in this country requires to be a sentence of two years in the penitentiary.
I do not know just exactly what the period is in England. As to this being a new

clause, it was omitted from our Act of 1919 but it was in the British Act of 1918 and was included in those amendments which the Imperial authorities submitted to the governments of the Dominions before they introduced the Bill. It is, therefore, one of the clauses which, if our legislation is to carry out the results of previous consultation, ought to be included in the Act. That does not mean that a man's certificate must be revoked in such case. Hon. members will notice the concluding clause of these enumerations;
And that (in any case) the continuance of the certificate is not conducive to the public good.
So that if the Governor in Council had no reason to consider that the maintenance of the certificate would be not conducive to the public good, the Governor in Council would be at perfect liberty not to revoke the certificate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-application to court.

What authorities are contemplated by the words:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman knows, the Northwest Territories are now very considerably reduced, and they have not any organized system of Government.
Would the power be vested in a commissioner, or would the Government appoint any particular tribunal to deal with this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think, in all probability, the power would be vested in a commissioner. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-issue of certificate of naturalization :

In the riding which I represent there were in 1918 some 90 or 93 men who made application and passed a judge, and their applications came to the Secretary of State but they have never been acted upon. Will it be necessary for these men to go through the whole procedure again and have their names posted up for
three months, or will their applications be accepted without any further formalities'?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before answering that
question absolutely, I should like to see how far the proceedings had gone.
I think it was done under an Order in Council1.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is not a matter
to be dealt with in my own department, so perhaps I should not undertake to speak for the minister who has the decision of the question and who would be mv hon. colleague the Secretary of State (Mr. Sifton). But my impression of the matter wmuld be that if all those formalities had been complied with and application was pending before the Secretary of State, calling only for action by him, his action would be impeded since ' last year by the enactment of the. section which dealt with the ten-year period, and which we are about to deal with in this Bill. If that obstacle be removed in the particular cases referred to by the legislation we are now dealing with, while, I say,
I cannot undertake offhand this evening to bind the minister concerned, it would seem to me that he would be entitled to go on and act upon the evidence already before him without requiring it to be made all over again.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 6-section 26 of the Act of 1914 repealed:
What is section 26?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is a section which last year disappeared from Ithe Act of 1914 by the legislation of 1919. It was a section in the third part of the Act of 1914 dealing with our own procedure and in no way connected with that portion which requires to be uniform. In the original Act there was a provision that commis-12 m. sioners might be appointed for purpose of taking oaths under thalt Act. Under section 24, which is reintroduced from the Act of 1919, the applicant is authorized to take the oath before any person duly authorized to administer judicial oaths by the laws of the province in which the applicant resides. That being so, the necessity for appointing commissioners especially to take oaths under this Act disappeared, and I think both the minister immediately concerned with the Bill of last year, and Parl'iament, thought it undesirable to have special commissioners

under this Act, and I must say I concur in this view. This is just to leave oaths under this Adt to be administered by officers who administer oaths generally.
On section 7-certificates granted to enemy subjects since 4th August, 1914:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The change is the addition of paragraph (d).

Subclause (2) establishes
whalt might be termed the ten-year probationary period for those of former alien enemy origin. While it permits naturalization of those who have previously lived in Canada for ten years, it does not make provision for those who may attain the full Iten-year residence in Canada after 1909. As this law stands now, the effect of it would be that any person of former alien enemy nationality who was resident in Canada on July 7, 1909, could now be naturalized, but a man who came to Canada in the fall of 1909, or in 1910, 1911, 1912, 1913, could nolt obtain naturalization until 1929. That is, he would have to go through a probation of from sixteen to twenty years. Such persons must wait until July 7, 1929, before they can be naturalized. lit would be fair to insert a provision that just so soon as a man of that kind has lived here for the full period of ten years, he should become eligible for naturalization. For instance, if he came Ito Canada in 1912, he should be eligible for naturalization in 1922. There should be even another provision made for exceptional cases, such provision, for example, as we find in the United States. If a man has not been there ten years the President has reserved Ito him the absolute right to grant him a certificate if his loyalty and general fitness are proved. Take for example the case of a man who came from the United States to Canada, having been away from Germany- and I know of an instance of this kind-for a good many years. He lived in the United States and took out his first papers, but he never completed his naturalization in the United States. He came to Canada, has not been here quite ten years and will not be eligible for naturalization.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Wlas he naturalized in the United States?
He had taken out his first papers only.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In answer to my hon. friend I may say that this particular subsection was taken practically verbatim out of an address of his own,-
I was going to mention that,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -in which he set forth what he at that time thought would be a proper measure. But, quite apart from that, I appeal to the hon. gentleman whether it is not a reasonable requirement on our part, in extending this exceptional opportunity, that the parties to. whom it is to be extended should have lived some period in this country before the war, and should during that period and during the war have had an opportunity of giving proof Of that loyalty, and so forth, which is required. I think the committee Will be unanimous on this point, that the provision that suspends for a time the naturalization of people who have just come into this country since the war is a proper precaution under the circumstances. Without any feeling of vindictiveness whatever, we must realize, I think, that this is only a necessary and proper precaution to 'take. After all, if we analysed our feelings towards those who were our enemies, and proceeded, in a not unfair process of reasoning, on the assumption that our enemies, being human like ourselves, might very probably entertain towards us the same kind of feelings that we have in respect of them, we would come to the conclusion that it was only fair to say to those coming after the war: "You should wait your ten years until we have had ample opportunity off judging of your conduct in the future." We are extending the benefit of citizenship to a certain class of people for whom exemption from the provisions of the law, as applicable to those who are coming in, is granted; and I do not think it is unfair to say that we should extend this benefit only to those whom we have had for ten years under our eye before the termination of the war. I do; not think that on reflection the hon. gentleman, whose zeal on behalf of those whom he represents I admire, will see that we have gone as far as we ought fairly to be asked to go, and that while cases of this class of people must appeal to every one's sympathy, we are after all acting as generously as we could be asked to act, by making this present provision. At all events, we are meeting the cases of all the people on whose behalf, up to this evening, I have heard any special appeal made.

The minister states that this clause was drafted practically according to an amendment I offered last year. That is true, and it was simply by an over-

sight on my (part that I did not make provision in my amendment last year-which did not carry after all-for those people of whom I am speaking. I am not accustomed to drafting laws, land (perhaps I might be excused in view of the fact that last year the statement was made that the British Act did not allow this clause to be accepted, whereas iwe find that the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie), the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) and even the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) were all wrong in their reading of that Act. I will point out that in the case of the people whose naturalization we have been discussing there is a double safeguard. After ail, they must run the gauntlet of an examination before the judge, and the application must pass the Secretary of State. So that if either of these two men had the slightest suspicion as to the loyalty or fitness of any man making an application he would simply turn him down, and there could be no possible danger. This fact will remain, that the man iwho came in prior to July 7, 1909, can obtain naturalization, but the man who came in August, 1909, has to wait until 1929, twenty years. That does not seem to be altogether fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps, as time goes on, iwe may have opportunity for giving further consideration to that suggestion. As to the contrast the hon. gentleman makes, the case of the man who has to iwait twenty years looks harsh only 'because of the consideration that we have extended to those who had been here the ten years required. It is rather discouraging to find that when you extend a consideration it is immediately used as an .argument to show what an awful hardship some one, whom your considration does not reach, is suffering. We have to draw the line somewhere if this clause is to. be enacted at all, and .wherever rwe draw that line it will maJce a difference of ten years between the man. on one side and the man on the other side of it. I think that, for the time being iat all events, the present amendment which iwe are making meets amply all the cases that have been pleaded to us. We haive met them absolutely, 'and we have reserved .merely this one precaution, that we should require ten years in the country after the war, or a corresponding ten years before the termination of the war. It might not have been unreasonable, and it would have balanced it, if we had said ten yeais before the beginning of the war. But rwe have counted the war years in the ten, so that we have left ourselves with a
very narrow maTgin after all. I think that on reflection my hon. friend will see, notwithstanding his highly creditable zeal for those whom he represents, that under conditions 'as they are .the provision we have made goes as far as we would .be justified in going. Now, the hon. gentleman seemed to think that an observation I made involved .something that might call for excuse on his part. I did not mean to make any criticism of him in (that regard, nor do I think 'there was occasion for excuse. I merely desired to point out that cases that appealed to the hon. gentleman in the first instance have been fully met, and I think we might he given a little time to think over whether we ought to entertain the further 'appeal -that is made this evening to extend this consideration.

Will paragraph
(b) subsection 2 of section 7 apply to a citizen of Alsace-Lorraine whose sympathy was with France and opposed to the enemy Government hut who was a subject of Germany?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I fancy that Alsace-Lorraine was the typical case that was in mind. During the war, once any French authority was prepared to vouch for the feelings of a citizen of Alsace-Lorraine, we never treated him as an alien enemy. It would apply to any person in that position.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the position of one particular class of people as it is affedted by this Act. There is a very large class of settlers in Western Canada who came in 1909 and 1910, and took up land with the full understanding that they could become citizens and receive their naturalization papers and patents after the expiration of a certain time. I think there has been some provision made to allow them to secure Ithe patents to their land. I think the Minister of the Interior (Mr" Meighen) said last year that was the intention of the Government. But still it appears very unfair to them to deny them the rights of .citizenship under the circumstances. Although they have to pay municipal taxes, no matter how progressive many of them are in the settlement no one is allowed to become a councillor or a school trustee if he is not a citizen. These people are at a great disadvantage through no fault of their own.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Of what nationality are they?
.3922
Any description of enemy; it might be Austrian, or any of the nationalities precluded for the coming citizen by this Act.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If they were Poles, or if they came from Czecho-Slovalria they would come in under this subsection.

I quite appreciate that, but still there remain a lot of people who came in believing that they were coming in under certain conditions which have not been recognized. The Act does not relieve them, I know some people who are very progressive but who have only been in the country for eight or nine years They have been prosperous and have greatly assisted in the development and the production of the country. Still they are put in a class by themselves. The President of the Privy Council told us the other night how the Mounted Police were used to travel amongst this very class of people and try to discover any cases of the use of seditious Language or any disloyal act but in none of the districts of East Edmonton or Victoria were they able to get a conviction. That is certainly a certificate that these people in the last ten years behaved loyally and well. These people cannot hold any public office, and at the .same time they are useful, progressive citizens and no fault has been found with them.

My hon.
friend is probably mistaken as to one feature of this case. The people he refers to are probably the ones who come from Galicia. They were under Austria at one time. Western Galicia is now classed as Polish territory, and all who came from that portion of Galicia under Polish dominion are able to get their naturalization papers without further difficulty. The only question that remains is as to those who came from Eastern Galicia and they are counted as alien enemies as they came from German Galicia. My hon. friend is mistaken as to the other class because they are capable of being naturalized as friends.

Where there
have been new territories created I have no doubt these people will be relieved, but it does not relieve their neighbours who may be just as good citizens.

Then if
Eastern Galicia does not belong to Ausltria it will be a question of the League of Nations to determine where Eastern Galicia shall

go. Eastern Galicia does not belong to Austria to-day but for the present those coming from Eastern Galicia are not being given their naturalization papers. All those who come from Western Galicia can be naturalized.
